doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Four-track Beatles records and whether more tracks help
summary: More digital tracks do not make better music; he explains bouncing tracks on Sgt. Pepper's and his dislike of compressed ear-bud sound.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So does unlimited digital tracks necessarily make for better music?

No. No. Because we made great records. The Beatles cut Sgt. Pepper’s on a four-track, I think synced to another four track. And it was the technique, if you had four tracks, track one might be like George Martin with the Beatles. Track one might be McCartney and Ringo. They’d mix the drums and the bass on track one. Track two might be — would be the guitars and the bass mixed together. But you had to get all those levels set before you recorded. And then here’s track one, bass and drums. All the drums. You know it came to the point where we were using eight tracks just to record drums, and still do. But mix the bass and drums, the guitars and keyboard, here’s a vocal on track three. You’d leave track four open. And then to open up new tracks you’d bounce it down they called it. You’d mix track one with track two — the bass, drums and the guitars, bounce them over to track four and you’d open up two tracks here to put whatever, background vocals, a sax or something that wasn’t on the date. And then you’d keep bouncing things. Of course in analog, every time you bounce from one track to another you lose a generation so the sound degrades a little bit. But that’s the only way you could do it. So that’s what they did like George Martin with the Beatles. Bouncing tracks to open up new tracks. Because if you listen to that stuff, obviously it’s multiple tracks of things. And that was when it was just four tracks, two four track machines synced together and eventually an eight track machine. But I don’t think they ever recorded — well maybe later, in the late 60s

before they broke up they may have been on a sixteen track. But now when you say does more tracks make it — no. But it just gives you more stuff to put on there and try to filter your way through. And somebody asked me today in this recording class, the sound now as opposed to then. I said well everybody now listens with ear buds through their cell phone or computer, and it has to be compressed so much. And that sound back then — in my home music room I’ve got 1969 JBL speakers this tall, and that’s the way I like to listen, like in the control room. I can’t stand this sound because it’s so compressed, and it’s squashed down. It’s totally different. But that’s all anybody — there’s no yardstick now like it used to be. You had to make your records sound as good as Tom Dowd in New York or Al Schmidt in LA or something like that.
